title: Hagia Sophia
hookLine: the church becomes a mosque, then a museum, then a mosque again, felt deeply by both faiths

lines: A DOME THAT SEEMS TO FLOAT.
ROUND PANELS: THE NAMES OF GOD.
cards: Step inside and look up. A dome so wide and so high it seems to float, held up, as an old description put it, as if hung from heaven by a chain.
A ring of windows runs around its base, so the light pours in just under the curve. Up on the walls, faces in gold mosaic: Mary, Christ, emperors.

Across from them, huge round panels in Arabic calligraphy, bearing the names of God, the Prophet and those close to him. One building, loved by people who pray in very different ways. Today: Hagia Sophia.

teach.b: Hagia Sophia is Greek for Holy Wisdom. The Byzantine emperor Justinian built it as the great church of Constantinople, where emperors were crowned and the liturgy was sung beneath that dome.

teach.h: A MOSQUE: MINARETS AND A MIHRAB.
teach.b: When Mehmed took the city, he went to Hagia Sophia, and it became a mosque. Friday prayer was held there. Minarets rose at its corners.
A mihrab was set in the wall to face Mecca, a little off the line of the old church. Over time, the Christian images were covered over, and the great calligraphy panels were hung.
For Ottoman Muslims, it became a sign that God had given them the city. For Orthodox Christians, its loss became a lasting grief. Much later, the Turkish Republic made it a museum.
The plaster came off some mosaics, and visitors of every faith walked in to look up.

teach.h: A MUSEUM, THEN A MOSQUE AGAIN.
teach.b: In recent years it was made a mosque again. Some Muslims celebrated. Some Christians, and others, grieved.
Today it is open to visitors outside prayer times, and the Christian images are veiled while prayer is held. The Qur'an speaks of houses of worship of more than one faith in the same breath.

teach.h: CHURCHES AND MOSQUES IN ONE VERSE.
teach.b: Among the places that would have been pulled down had God not held some people back by others, it names, in Pickthall's translation, "cloisters and churches and oratories and mosques, wherein the name of Allah is oft mentioned".
Commentators differ over whether that last phrase means all four, or the mosques alone. This lesson doesn't settle the argument. It asks only that both griefs and both joys be heard.

how: Hagia Sophia is used today as a mosque for the five daily prayers and Friday prayer, and it stays open to visitors of every faith outside prayer times.

games.q: you look after Hagia Sophia as a mosque. gold mosaics of Mary and Christ are on the walls, and prayer is about to begin. what do you do?
o: veil the images while prayer is held.
leave everything exactly as it is.
games.why: today the Christian images are veiled during prayer, and visitors of every faith can see the building outside prayer times.

practice: Bring back the dome, the gold faces and the great round names, all under the same light. Then picture someone whose faith isn't yours, someone who shares your city or loves a place you love, standing beside you under that dome.
If you pray, ask in your own words for respect between faiths; if not, simply wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Hagia Sophia. Holy Wisdom: a great church, then a mosque, then a museum, and a mosque again, loved and grieved by Christians and Muslims alike. Today's word.
